  • Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine also spoke; a large American flag was unfurled on the building's west face.
  • Trump called the attacks a moment of immense evil and linked the anniversary to the present, saying the country is being tested again.
  • Vice President JD Vance attended the New York ceremony on the plaza where the Twin Towers stood, alongside all four living former presidents.
  • Ceremonies also took place in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, and at memorials across the country.

Left view

The Washington Post and CNN coverage notes the choice of venue — the Pentagon over ground zero — and, more substantively, questions the rhetorical link between the anniversary and the current war with Iran, a country not involved in the 2001 attacks. The broader retrospective theme on the left is the cost of the post-9/11 wars and how little of it was ever reckoned with.

Right view

Fox News and ABC's coverage lead on the commemoration itself and on continuity of purpose — the unity of the days after the attacks and the argument that the threat never went away. The connection Trump drew to Iran is treated on the right as the natural throughline rather than as a category error.

Watch for

Nothing operational, but the framing matters politically: a quarter-century mark arriving in the middle of another Middle East war gives both parties a template. Expect the "forever wars" argument to resurface in midterm messaging on the anti-interventionist right as much as on the left.

Sources: Washington Post ABC News / AP CNN Fox News

Markets & Economy

  • S&P 500: +0.86% to 7,656.98. Dow: +509.19 (+0.98%) to 52,573.29. Nasdaq: +0.96% to 26,333.04 — a four-session losing streak snapped as the CPI print landed near expectations and oil pulled back.
  • Oil: Brent settled around $104 after spiking past $108 intraday on the Perim Island news; WTI closed near $100, down about 2.4% on the day after Iran said Oman would host Gulf talks on Hormuz shipping. Saudi August output was the lowest since 1990.
  • Gas: AAA national average about $4.30 a gallon, up from $4.17 a week ago and roughly 32% higher than a year ago. Diesel is at a record near $5.94. Brown University researchers put the cumulative extra fuel cost since February at over $101 billion, roughly $777 per household.
  • Fed: FOMC decides Wednesday, September 16. Rates have been at 3.50%–3.75% all year; markets put a quarter-point hike at better-than-even odds.
  • Fiscal: Deficit at $1.97 trillion through 11 months; interest costs at a record $1.4 trillion.

Sports Watercooler

  • Golf: Quiet week on the PGA Tour — the postseason is done and the next event is the Biltmore Championship at The Cliffs at Walnut Cove in Asheville, September 17–20. The DP World Tour's Amgen Irish Open carried the weekend.
  • Tennis: Davis Cup qualifiers run September 18–20, with 14 teams playing for seven Finals spots. Holger Rune returns from injury for Denmark against Bulgaria in Copenhagen; Great Britain named Cam Norrie, Arthur Fery, Henry Patten and Lloyd Glasspool to face Ecuador. Laver Cup follows in London, September 25–27.
  • Squash: The QTerminals Qatar Classic — the season's first Platinum event — opens in Doha today and runs through September 18. Paul Coll took the London Squash Classic at Alexandra Palace earlier this month for his 28th PSA title, beating Joel Makin in three; Amina Orfi won the women's draw.
  • WWE: Sami Zayn beat CM Punk in Mexico City to take the Undisputed WWE Championship — a genuinely chaotic SmackDown from Arena CDMX. Chelsea Green retained against Nia Jax, Rey Fenix kept the AAA Cruiserweight Title over Ricky Saints, and the Viking Raiders won the AAA Tag Team Titles. Randy Orton opened the show calling his shot at title No. 15.
  • Hockey: Rookie camps are underway — the Flyers opened theirs in Allentown Friday. Detroit will start the season without a captain after Dylan Larkin relinquished the C, and the Red Wings still have no GM two months after firing Steve Yzerman. Vegas extended Braeden Bowman six years at $3.4M AAV; Alex Formenton signed a one-year deal in Edmonton.
  • Soccer: Premier League matchday four today — Liverpool host Fulham at Anfield and Aston Villa take Nottingham Forest at Villa Park, with the Manchester derby at Old Trafford tomorrow. The Champions League league phase is underway, with the final set for the Metropolitano in Madrid on June 5.
  • Football: College Week 2 is the headliner: No. 1 Ohio State at No. 4 Texas tonight, 7:30 ET on ABC. Also No. 11 Oklahoma at Michigan, No. 6 Oregon at Oklahoma State, Arizona State at No. 10 Texas A&M, Rice at Notre Dame on NBC, and Iowa–Iowa State. NFL Week 2 kicks off tomorrow.

item.title: Fri Sep 11, 2026 — Houthis seize Mocha, tightening their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb strait
item.description: Houthis seize Mocha, tightening their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb strait · Supreme Court blocks Missouri's Republican-drawn House map for the second time this week · Trump's $5,000 "dividend" pledge draws bipartisan pushback · Protections for about 200,000 Salvadorans left in limbo as DHS delays a decision
item.content:encoded:
The Big Stories Today

Houthis seize Mocha, tightening their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb strait

Facts

  • Iran-aligned Houthi forces took the Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday and pushed toward high ground overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb strait, about 50 miles away.
  • The corridor carries roughly 10% of global trade and by most estimates 5–7% of seaborne oil. It had become the main workaround for Gulf crude after the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed to routine commercial traffic in July.
  • The Houthis have declared a blockade aimed at Saudi-linked shipping and said the strait is closed to specified vessels.
  • Brent traded above $107 Thursday before easing; Hormuz traffic is down from more than 100 vessels a day before the war to roughly five, with Gulf crude exports off about 47% from 2025 levels.

Left view

MSNBC's opinion desk calls the seizure a much bigger deal than the administration is letting on and argues the Iran campaign has produced exactly the escalation critics warned about. NPR and CNN emphasize that roughly 45 days of U.S. strikes on the Houthis last year did not degrade the group's ability to project force, and that the White House has no stated plan beyond more bombing.

Right view

RedState and the Washington Times frame it as proof that Iran's proxy network survives because Washington keeps stopping short — the argument being that limited strikes invite this. The Wall Street Journal editorial line has been that freedom of navigation requires a standing naval commitment, not episodic retaliation. Reason and other libertarian-leaning outlets take the opposite tack on the right, noting the Houthi campaign has already cost taxpayers north of $1 billion with little to show.

Watch for

Energy analysts see Brent staying in a $100–110 band while both chokepoints are contested; some forecasters have Brent averaging around $106 for 2026. Watch war-risk insurance premiums on Red Sea transits, Suez Canal transit volumes, and whether Saudi Arabia leans harder on the East–West pipeline to Yanbu. Bank of America has estimated sustained oil above $100 shaves more than 60 basis points off U.S. GDP growth. A U.S. or Saudi move to retake Mocha is the tail risk that would spike prices further.

Sources: CNN CNBC Times of Israel Al Jazeera MSNBC Opinion RedState

Supreme Court blocks Missouri's Republican-drawn House map for the second time this week

Facts

  • The justices on Thursday paused a federal judge's order that would have required Missouri to use a new 7–1 Republican-favoring congressional map in November.
  • The existing 6–2 map drawn after the 2020 census stays in effect for the general election while litigation continues.
  • Last week the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously blocked the Trump-backed map and ordered the question put to a statewide referendum, setting up the conflict between state and federal rulings.
  • The fight sits downstream of Louisiana v. Callais, the 6–3 decision in April narrowing when the Voting Rights Act can compel additional majority-minority districts.

Left view

The Washington Post and Democracy Docket present this as a rare speed bump in a redistricting wave the Court itself opened, with tallies suggesting Republicans could net well into double digits in House seats from post-Callais map redraws. NBC News reports on mounting criticism that the Court is intervening in election cases too close to voting.

Right view

Conservative legal commentators, including at National Review and The Dispatch, argue the ruling is procedurally correct rather than a defeat — the Purcell principle counsels against changing rules near an election, and it cuts both ways. Fox News coverage stresses that Missouri Republicans were following a legislature's prerogative and that Democratic states including California and Virginia have run the same play.

Watch for

Election forecasters were already treating House control as close to a coin flip; holding Missouri at 6–2 removes one seat from the GOP column. Watch the Missouri referendum timing, whether Georgia and Tennessee maps draw similar emergency applications, and whether the Court takes the Missouri case on the merits after November.

Sources: Washington Post NBC News The Hill PBS NewsHour CFR

Trump's $5,000 "dividend" pledge draws bipartisan pushback

Facts

  • Closing the first-ever Republican midterm convention in Dallas Wednesday night, Trump promised every U.S. adult a $5,000 payment if the GOP holds both chambers in November.
  • He did not specify a funding source. Applied to roughly 270 million adults, the cost would exceed $1.3 trillion.
  • Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said he would draft legislation after the November 3 election. Former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.) called it a socialist vote-buying scheme.
  • Trump also predicted at the convention that the war with Iran would end shortly after the election.

Left view

CNBC and NBC News lead on the fiscal math and on legal questions about conditioning payments on an election outcome; Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) said nobody believes the checks are coming. The Guardian and Vox frame the pledge as an admission that affordability is the GOP's weakest issue heading into November.

Right view

Fox News reports open division inside the party, with fiscal conservatives objecting to a new entitlement layered on the debt. National Review and The Dispatch have been dismissive on the same grounds. The supportive case, made by Moreno and parts of the populist right, is that tariff revenue should be rebated to households rather than absorbed by Washington.

Watch for

Economists across the spectrum flag the inflation risk of a $1.3 trillion transfer with CPI already near 3.4% and oil above $100. Watch whether any actual bill text appears before Election Day, how the Congressional Budget Office scores it if so, and whether Treasury yields — the 10-year hit its highest level since 2023 on Thursday — keep pricing in looser fiscal policy.

Sources: CNBC Fox News The Hill NPR PBS NewsHour

Protections for about 200,000 Salvadorans left in limbo as DHS delays a decision

Facts

  • Temporary Protected Status for Salvadorans was set to expire September 9. DHS instead said the status remains in effect until further notice, without formally extending it.
  • Roughly 200,000 people are covered, many of them in the U.S. for two decades or more.
  • Since January 2025 the administration has ended or moved to end TPS for 13 countries, affecting more than a million people, including Haitians and Syrians.
  • Reporting points to the relationship between Trump and Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele — who has accepted U.S. deportees — as a distinguishing factor.

Left view

The Washington Post and NBC News center the human cost of indefinite limbo: work authorization that could lapse without notice, mortgages, and U.S.-citizen children. The Guardian and Mother Jones argue the selective treatment shows TPS decisions are being driven by diplomatic favor-trading rather than the statutory country-conditions test.

Right view

The Washington Times and the New York Post note that "temporary" status lasting 25 years is the anomaly the administration is trying to unwind, and that Congress, not DHS, should decide permanent legal status. The Free Press and Reason split from that: both have argued that abruptly stripping status from long-settled workers is bad policy on economic grounds regardless of the original designation.

Watch for

A Federal Register notice is the trigger to watch — it would set the wind-down clock. Also watch litigation in the Ninth Circuit, where earlier TPS terminations were challenged, and whether the delay holds past November. Construction and hospitality labor markets in Texas, Virginia, Maryland and California are the most exposed.

Sources: Washington Post NBC News UPI Washington Times

IAEA says North Korea has built a second enrichment plant at Yongbyon

Facts

  • The IAEA reported a new two-story building at the Yongbyon complex capable of housing up to 28 centrifuge cascades, identified by matching state-media photos of a June Kim Jong Un visit against satellite imagery.
  • An expanded annex at the Kangson site near Pyongyang also appears to be operating.
  • Construction started in mid-to-late 2024; the shell was finished by mid-2025 with internal installation continuing.
  • The agency has had no inspectors in the country since 2009. Director General Rafael Grossi called the expansion of weapons-grade material production a serious concern and said it violates U.N. Security Council resolutions.

Left view

NPR and The Atlantic treat this as evidence that summit-driven diplomacy without verification produced nothing durable, and argue the absence of inspectors since 2009 is the core failure. Reuters and CNN coverage stresses that Pyongyang's program has expanded through three U.S. administrations.

Right view

National Review and the Washington Examiner point to the report as an argument against sanctions relief in advance of verified dismantlement, and press for tighter enforcement on Chinese entities facilitating trade. Some on the right also note the U.S. is stretched across Iran and the Red Sea, leaving little bandwidth for the Korean peninsula.

Watch for

Analysts expect this to feed South Korea's domestic debate over its own deterrent and to strengthen the case in Tokyo for higher defense spending. Watch the IAEA Board of Governors meeting response, any U.S. force-posture signaling in the region, and whether Beijing acknowledges the findings at all.

Sources: CNN Japan Times Seoul Economic Daily

Twenty-five years on from 9/11, a divided country marks the anniversary

Facts

  • The commemoration at the National September 11 Memorial began at 8:30 a.m. ET with an in-person reading of the names by family members and the first moment of silence at 8:46 a.m.
  • Seven moments of silence mark each tower strike and collapse, the Pentagon attack, the Flight 93 crash, and those who have died since from 9/11-related illness.
  • Ceremonies are also being held at the Pentagon in Arlington and at the Flight 93 memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
  • A live broadcast of the Tribute in Light from Lower Manhattan airs at 8 p.m. ET. The anniversary also falls a day after the one-year mark of Charlie Kirk's assassination; his accused killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and faces trial.

Left view

NPR's framing is that a country that briefly unified in 2001 now gathers to remember while split on nearly everything else, including what the post-9/11 wars accomplished. The Atlantic and Vox have used the quarter-century mark to revisit the surveillance and detention architecture built after the attacks and how much of it remains.

Right view

The Washington Times and New York Post emphasize the first responders, the compensation fund, and the continuing toll of 9/11-related illness. National Review's anniversary coverage argues the counterterrorism apparatus is the reason there has been no comparable attack on U.S. soil, and warns against dismantling it.

Watch for

Practical items rather than predictions: the World Trade Center Health Program's funding position, the pace of Guantanamo military-commission proceedings for the accused plotters, and how much airtime the anniversary shares with the Red Sea and midterm news cycles.

Sources: NPR 9/11 Memorial NewsNation Washington Times

Markets & Economy

  • S&P 500: closed down 0.58% Thursday, a fourth straight losing day. Dow: off 0.6%. Nasdaq: off 0.65%. Futures were pointing higher Friday morning — Dow futures up about 299 points, S&P and Nasdaq-100 futures each up roughly 0.6% — as crude pulled back. (CNBC, Yahoo Finance, TheStreet)
  • Oil: Brent around $106 Friday morning, down about 1.4% on the day after topping $107 Thursday on the Mocha news; WTI near $99, off 3.3%. Gulf crude exports are running near 9 million bpd versus about 17 million in 2025. (Trading Economics, Reuters)
  • Gas: AAA national average $4.27 a gallon, up 13 cents in a week on the crude run-up. New Jersey is at $4.36. (AAA Newsroom, ROI-NJ)
  • Rates and other: Fed funds still 3.50–3.75% after repeated holds; futures put near-certain odds on no cuts this year, with Chair Kevin Warsh signaling a hawkish hold and some FOMC members open to hikes. CPI is running near 3.4% y/y; August payrolls came in at 162,000 with unemployment at 4.1%. The 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest since 2023 Thursday. Moody's Analytics now puts 12-month recession odds near 50%; Goldman Sachs is around 30%. (Bloomberg, CNBC, Trading Economics)

Sports Watercooler

  • Golf: Presidents Cup rosters are set for Medinah, September 24–27. Brandt Snedeker's U.S. picks — Xander Schauffele, Justin Thomas, Patrick Cantlay, Chris Gotterup, Jacob Bridgeman and 21-year-old Jackson Koivun — join automatic qualifiers Scottie Scheffler, Cameron Young, Wyndham Clark, Russell Henley, Sam Burns and Collin Morikawa. Koivun turned pro this spring and won the 3M Open in his third start. Geoff Ogilvy's International side added Corey Conners, Sungjae Im, Nico Echavarria, Ryo Hisatsune, Nick Taylor and Christiaan Bezuidenhout. The U.S. has won 10 straight. (PGA Tour, Golf Digest)
  • Tennis: The US Open women's final is set — Elena Rybakina, the new world No. 1, against Aryna Sabalenka, after Rybakina came back on Coco Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4 and Sabalenka handled Jessica Pegula 7-5, 6-2. Men's semifinals go today: Ben Shelton vs. Frances Tiafoe, Alexander Zverev vs. Karen Khachanov. (CBS Sports, Olympics.com)
  • Squash: The QTerminals Qatar Classic, the season's first Platinum event, runs September 12–18 in Doha. Paul Coll and Amina Orfi took the London Squash Classic titles at Alexandra Palace earlier this month; Coll beat Joel Makin in the men's final. (PSA Squash Tour)
  • WWE: CM Punk defends the Undisputed WWE Championship against Sami Zayn in Mexico City on SmackDown tonight, a week after surviving Johnny Gargano with Zayn interfering. WWE added eight Raw and SmackDown dates for November and December; tickets go on general sale this morning. (WWE.com, Fightful)
  • Hockey: Training camps open September 16–17 with the season starting September 29. Connor Hellebuyck's situation in Winnipeg is still unresolved, Alex DeBrincat has made his intentions known in Detroit, Quinn Hughes remains without a long-term extension in Minnesota, and Sidney Crosby is talking about another deal in Pittsburgh. Vancouver committed big money to 20-year-old defenseman Zeev Buium. (Bleacher Report, NHL Trade Rumors)
  • Soccer: The 2026-27 Champions League league phase opened September 8. Premier League clubs return from the international break for a matchweek on September 19–20 that includes Brighton–Arsenal, Tottenham–Aston Villa and Manchester City–Sunderland. (BBC Sport, Premier League)
  • Football: The 49ers beat the Rams 27-7 at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in the NFL's first regular-season game in Australia — San Francisco arrived a week early to adjust and it showed. Week 1 continues through Sunday; Week 2 opens September 17 with Lions at Bills. (NBC Sports, ESPN)

item.title: Thu Sep 10, 2026 — Trump promises every adult a $5,000 check if Republicans hold Congress
item.description: Trump promises every adult a $5,000 check if Republicans hold Congress · Brent tops $100 after US destroys five Iranian tankers; Trump says the war ends after the midterms · Trump asks the Supreme Court a third time to let the USPS mail-ballot rule take effect · UK bans West Bank settlement imports and cites “ethnic cleansing”; Israel retaliates
item.content:encoded:
The Big Stories Today

Trump promises every adult a $5,000 check if Republicans hold Congress

Facts

  • Speaking Wednesday night at the RNC's midterm convention in Dallas, Trump pledged to issue a $5,000 “dividend” to every adult US citizen if Republicans keep both the House and the Senate in November.
  • He offered no funding mechanism, comparing it to a corporate shareholder dividend and to the $1,776 bonus payments his administration sent military members last year, and suggested tariff revenue could cover part of it.
  • NBC's Garrett Haake put the arithmetic at roughly 269 million adults, or about $1.35 trillion — on top of an annual deficit already near $1.8 trillion. Any such payment would require an act of Congress.
  • The convention is an unusual format: a Trump-centered party gathering in a non-presidential year, which the RNC says raised nearly $55 million. Embattled Senate candidates from Texas and Georgia also spoke.

Left view

CNN and CBS News framed the pledge as the headline takeaway of a convention built around Trump personally, and emphasized the missing price tag and the congressional approval it would need. Left-leaning commentators went further and called it vote-buying outright — Raw Story catalogued critics describing it as a “bribe,” and the broader critique is that conditioning a cash payment on an election outcome is a transactional use of the Treasury, arriving just as tariffs have raised consumer prices.

Right view

Fox News led with the promise as a “first-of-its-kind” play to energize a base facing a difficult map, treating it as a bold closing argument on the economy rather than a policy proposal. Notably, the skepticism was not confined to the left: Fox's own Jacqui Heinrich pointed out on air that Trump has floated voter payments before — including a $2,000 tariff dividend last year — without delivering. Deficit-focused conservatives have been the loudest critics of the cost.

Watch for

Budget analysts expect this to stay rhetorical; a payment this size has no obvious path through a Congress already struggling on appropriations. The more testable effects are political: whether GOP candidates in tight races adopt the pledge or dodge it, and whether Senate Republicans worried about the deficit are forced to say publicly what they think. Markets largely ignored it — bond desks have been focused on oil and the Fed — but a credible $1.3 trillion transfer would be an inflation story, which is exactly the wrong backdrop three weeks after a hawkish Jackson Hole.

Sources: CNN CBS News Fox News Euronews Raw Story

Brent tops $100 after US destroys five Iranian tankers; Trump says the war ends after the midterms

Facts

  • Brent crude closed above $100 a barrel Wednesday for the first time since May, trading near $101 Thursday. WTI for October was around $96.
  • Central Command said US forces destroyed five Iranian crude tankers Tuesday, in retaliation for two failed Iranian attempts to strike a US Navy warship.
  • Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched missiles and drones at four southern Saudi cities, sparking fires at oil facilities. A separate report said several US aircraft were damaged in Iran's strike on a US airbase in Jordan.
  • Trump said at the Dallas convention that the war will “end immediately” after the November 3 midterms, arguing Tehran is holding out to influence the result. The conflict, which began February 28, is in its seventh month.
  • Reporting indicates White House advisers have privately raised with Trump the possibility the war runs through the rest of his term.

Left view

NBC News and NPR have centered the cost to households — pump prices up roughly a dollar in a month — and the absence of a stated war aim or exit condition after seven months. The left-leaning read of Trump's “ends after the midterms” line is that it concedes the timing is political: if the war can be stopped on November 4, the question is why it is still running on September 10.

Right view

The right is split, and unusually openly. The Washington Examiner reported the midterm claim straight but has run op-eds arguing the campaign is strategic overreach the US cannot afford, one explicitly comparing it to Bush-era hubris. National Review has published a run of pieces — “The Iran War Is Eating Trump's Presidency,” “Trump Doesn't Have the Stomach for a Long War” — arguing public opposition is constraining him. The Daily Caller and Washington Times covered the tanker strikes as a demonstration of resolve. Hawks maintain that degrading Iran's export capacity is the point; restrainers counter that $100 oil is Tehran's best weapon and the US just helped fire it.

Watch for

Goldman Sachs has said Brent could top $120 next quarter and average above $100 next year if Strait of Hormuz flows stay severely restricted, against a base case nearer $85. JPMorgan is the outlier, holding a roughly $60 baseline on the view that long disruptions are unlikely — a wide analyst spread that itself signals how much depends on shipping. Sustained $100+ crude feeds directly into the Fed's September 16 decision and into pump prices heading into voting season. Watch tanker insurance rates and Hormuz transit volumes, which move before prices do.

Sources: CNBC NBC News Washington Examiner National Review Washington Times Energy Connects

Trump asks the Supreme Court a third time to let the USPS mail-ballot rule take effect

Facts

  • The Justice Department filed an emergency application Sunday asking the Supreme Court to let the Postal Service implement its new ballot-mail rule before the midterms — the third time the administration has taken the matter to the justices.
  • The rule, published in the Federal Register on August 26 and stemming from a March 31 executive order, requires states to upload each mail voter's name and address to a federal portal, tied to a unique barcode. Carriers would deliver ballots only to voters on the state-supplied list.
  • USPS says it will not determine eligibility, maintain voter rolls, or count ballots, and that no birthdates or Social Security numbers go into the portal.
  • US District Judge Indira Talwani blocked the rule, finding that implementing it fewer than 70 days before the election risks disenfranchising millions and that the record contained no evidence of mail-voting fraud justifying the speed.
  • North Carolina and parts of Wisconsin began mailing absentee ballots last week; more states start this month.

Left view

NPR and the ACLU frame this as an administrative obstacle inserted mid-election with no fraud record behind it, and lean on Talwani's finding about the timing. The specific worry is mechanical rather than theoretical: if a state's upload is incomplete or a name is mismatched, a lawfully requested ballot simply is not delivered, and the voter may not learn why until it is too late to cure.

Right view

The executive order's own language, echoed by supporters, is that unique envelope identifiers confirm only citizens receive ballots. A 13-state coalition led by Alabama's attorney general argued in comments that the rule would help combat fraud, and supporters told USPS that better tracking would expose discrepancies between ballots sent and returned. The Washington Examiner has covered the litigation as the administration being repeatedly blocked on a modest chain-of-custody measure. National Review-adjacent election writers have been more cautious, noting that changing rules this close to voting invites the chaos both sides claim to want to avoid.

Watch for

The Court already let parts of the underlying executive order proceed in August, so the shadow-docket posture matters more than the merits right now. Election administrators expect that if the justices grant relief, states mid-stream in mailing ballots face the hardest operational problem — and litigation over individual undelivered ballots becomes likely in close races. A denial effectively shelves the rule until after November.

Sources: NPR NBC News SCOTUSblog Washington Examiner Federal Register

UK bans West Bank settlement imports and cites “ethnic cleansing”; Israel retaliates

Facts

  • Britain announced a ban on imports originating in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband saying settlers are carrying out ethnic cleansing and restating that the settlements are illegal under international law.
  • Canada and France said they will impose similar bans; Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal and Sweden pledged support for further action — twelve states in all.
  • Israel responded by barring 12 British MPs and ordering the British consulate in Jerusalem closed within 30 days. The UK is defending the sanctions.
  • Foreign ministers of Türkiye and seven other countries welcomed the move Thursday.

Left view

The Guardian and Al Jazeera cast this as overdue rather than dramatic — a first concrete step after the UK recognized a Palestinian state last year, and one that follows existing UK legal position rather than breaking new ground. An ECFR poll cited by Al Jazeera found 72% of Britons back the trade ban when “don't knows” are excluded.

Right view

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, writing in The Sun, called the measures performative politics aimed at Labour MPs and activists regardless of the consequences for Britain. The wider right-of-center objection is about proportion and leverage: settlement goods are a small share of UK–Israel trade, so the ban costs Britain a consulate and diplomatic access while changing little on the ground. US coverage on the right has emphasized the split it opens between London and Washington.

Watch for

The consequential number is how many of the twelve states convert pledges into actual customs rules, and whether the EU takes it up as a bloc — that is the difference between a symbolic measure and a real trade instrument. Also watch whether Israel escalates beyond the consulate closure, and whether the Trump administration publicly breaks with London, which would be the first significant US–UK rift of this term.

Sources: Washington Post NPR NBC News Al Jazeera CNBC

Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect as the trade fight widens

Facts

  • Canadian retaliatory tariffs of 15% to 50% took effect at 12:01 a.m. ET Tuesday on roughly C$27.6 billion (about US$20 billion) of American goods, including steel, household appliances, agricultural equipment and dairy. Ottawa paired them with support for affected domestic businesses.
  • The measures answer a US 50% levy on about $20 billion of Canadian goods imposed after talks broke down in late August.
  • The White House responded with presidential actions banning imports of many Canadian dairy products, motorcycles and alcoholic beverages beginning September 29.
  • Analysts cited the escalation as one of the drags on US equities Wednesday alongside oil and yields.

Left view

Al Jazeera and center-left economics coverage stress that the targets are consumer-facing — appliances, food, alcohol — so the incidence lands on households in both countries, and that the collapse of talks damaged a relationship that took decades to build. Prime Minister Carney's subsidy package is read as an admission that the tariffs hurt Canadians too.

Right view

Supporters of the administration's approach argue Canada's dairy supply-management system and digital-services measures were longstanding grievances the US finally priced, and that Ottawa blinked into retaliation rather than concede. Free-trade conservatives at outlets like Reason and the WSJ editorial page have been consistently hostile to the whole exercise, arguing tariffs are taxes on Americans and that a 50% levy on an allied economy is self-harm dressed as leverage.

Watch for

September 29 is the next hard date — the US import bans take effect then, and they hit categories with concentrated Canadian supply. Watch auto-parts and steel supply chains, where cross-border content rules make tariffs compound, and watch whether either side reopens talks before the US bans bite. Bank economists have flagged the dispute as a modest but real drag on Q4 North American growth, arriving alongside an oil shock.

Sources: Al Jazeera CNBC Congressional Research Service TheStreet

Russian drone nearly hit Zelensky's plane leaving Moldova

Facts

  • A suspected Russian Shahed-type drone that violated Moldovan and Romanian airspace Tuesday came close to the aircraft carrying Volodymyr Zelensky as it departed Chisinau.
  • Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre disclosed the incident. Zelensky was traveling to Oslo for the funeral of King Harald V.
  • Moldova closed its airspace Tuesday afternoon, delaying three departures including Zelensky's. A drone crashed in a sunflower field in the Riscani district, starting four fires; no injuries were reported.
  • Moldova's ambassador to the US, Vladislav Kulminski, told CNN the incident was likely not an accident.

Left view

The Washington Post and European center-left coverage place this in a pattern of Russian airspace violations testing NATO and near-NATO responses, and argue it strengthens the case for extending air defense coverage over Moldova and Romania rather than treating each incursion as an isolated navigation error.

Right view

Right-leaning coverage of this one has been thin in the US — the Iran war and the convention are absorbing the attention — which is worth flagging. Where it has appeared, the framing is that Moscow escalates precisely when Washington is distracted, and hawks use it to argue against any settlement that leaves Russian strike capability intact. Restrainers on the right read the same facts as a reason to keep the US out of a second theater.

Watch for

Whether NATO members formally raise the incursion, and whether Romania invokes consultations. Moldova's airspace closures are becoming routine, which has practical consequences for civil aviation routing around the Black Sea. Also watch whether Kyiv uses the incident to press for longer-range air defense in ongoing talks over the US-brokered proposal shuttled between Moscow and Kyiv this month.

Sources: Washington Post Kyiv Independent MS NOW

Markets & Economy

  • S&P 500: 7,636.36, −0.48%. Dow: 52,380.66, −405.41 (−0.77%). Nasdaq: 26,253.34, −0.64%. Wednesday was broadly risk-off — oil, yields, Iran and the Canada trade fight all pulling the same direction. The Russell 2000 and VIX moves were the tell: small caps led losses, volatility bid.
  • Oil: Brent above $101 after closing over $100 Wednesday, first time since May; WTI October futures around $96. Goldman sees $120+ next quarter if Hormuz stays disrupted; JPMorgan is holding a roughly $60 baseline, an unusually wide split.
  • Gas: AAA national average about $4.22/gal as of September 9, up roughly a dollar in a month. California is highest near $5.81; Indiana lowest around $3.45. Pump prices lag crude by two to three weeks, so the tanker-strike move has not fully arrived yet.
  • Rates: Long-end Treasury yields set new 52-week highs; the 10-year touched 4.80% earlier this month, its highest since November 2023. The Fed decides September 16 with the funds range at 3.50–3.75%; markets put a 25bp hike near a coin flip after Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole address, a full reversal from the cuts economists penciled in earlier this year. Three FOMC members already dissented for a hike in July.
  • Other: The $5,000 dividend pledge is not in anyone's forecasts; a genuine $1.3 trillion transfer would be an inflation event on top of an oil shock. Deficit is running near $1.8 trillion annually.

Sports Watercooler

  • Golf: Solheim Cup week at Bernardus Golf in North Brabant, Netherlands, with matches running through Sunday. On the men's side the Procore Championship in Napa opens the fall calendar. Off the course, LIV Golf is in Chapter 11 with more than $500 million in debt, seeking a smaller player-owned structure — 14 players sit among its 30 largest unsecured creditors.
  • Tennis: An all-American men's semifinal at the US Open Friday — No. 8 Ben Shelton against No. 11 Frances Tiafoe — guaranteeing an American in the final. Shelton ended Carlos Alcaraz's title defense 6-7(5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6(10-7) in a match that finished at 3:33 a.m. ET, the latest in tournament history. Women's semis: Sabalenka vs. Pegula and Gauff vs. Rybakina — first time since 1975 all four top seeds have reached the US Open semifinals. Record $108M purse, up 21% on 2025.
  • Squash: The QTerminals Qatar Classic in Doha, the season's first Platinum event, runs September 12–18. Paul Coll took the London Squash Classic at Alexandra Palace for his 28th PSA title (13-11, 11-7, 11-8); Amina Orfi won the women's draw. The PSA has 24 World Events across 14 countries scheduled through December.
  • WWE: CM Punk retained the Undisputed WWE Title over Johnny Gargano last Friday despite Sami Zayn's interference, then challenged Zayn to a title match in Mexico City. Chelsea Green vs. Nia Jax is set for the Women's Championship. Next PLEs: Worlds Collide September 26, Money in the Bank October 10, Crown Jewel November 7.
  • Hockey: Rookie camps are open with showcase tournaments September 11–15; most veteran camps start September 17–20 (Canucks in Penticton, Blues and Flyers on the 17th). Preseason games begin September 19 and the regular season opens September 29 — earlier than usual because it is the first 84-game schedule, which is putting conditioning and depth at the center of camp. Toronto took Gavin McKenna first overall in June and signed Sergei Bobrovsky to three years.
  • Soccer: The Champions League league phase opened Tuesday, so the second slate of matchday-one fixtures runs this week. Europa League starts September 16, AFC Champions League Elite September 14, Women's Champions League September 22.
  • Football: Seahawks 13, Patriots 10 in Wednesday's kickoff game — a Super Bowl LX rematch that Seattle won on a Jason Myers 26-yard field goal with 5:53 left after trailing 7-0 at half. Drake Maye threw three interceptions. Tonight: 49ers–Rams in Australia. Sunday brings Chiefs–Broncos and the possible return of Patrick Mahomes.

item.title: Wed Sep 9, 2026 — US destroys five Iranian tankers; Tehran hits Jordan base as the “tanker war” widens
item.description: US destroys five Iranian tankers; Tehran hits Jordan base as the “tanker war” widens · Brent touches $100 and gas sets a September record — and the Fed is now expected to hike · Canada's counter-tariffs take effect on roughly $20B of American goods · Twelve countries move to ban Israeli settlement goods; Israel closes the UK consulate in East Jerusalem
item.content:encoded:
The Big Stories Today

US destroys five Iranian tankers; Tehran hits Jordan base as the “tanker war” widens

Facts

  • CENTCOM says US forces struck five Iranian oil tankers in the latest round of tit-for-tat attacks, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired ballistic missiles toward a US carrier and destroyer near the Strait of Hormuz. No US ships were hit and no servicemembers injured, per the Pentagon.
  • Iran retaliated with strikes on a US base in Jordan and on commercial vessels it says are US-linked, according to Al Jazeera and ABC News. Iranian officials report at least 11 dead and dozens wounded from US strikes in southern Iran.
  • The exchanges follow a “tanker for tanker” policy Trump approved in early September, first reported by Axios. Secretary of State Marco Rubio framed it as a standing rule: Iranian attacks on US ships cost Iran tankers.
  • The war began Feb. 28 with joint US–Israeli strikes; Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in response. An April 7 ceasefire lapsed. Hormuz traffic is down from roughly 100 vessels a day to about five, per Al Jazeera's shipping analysis.
  • Gulf crude exports have fallen roughly 47%, from about 17 million barrels a day in 2025 to roughly 9 million bpd as of August.

Left view

NPR and The Guardian keep the focus on legal authority: seven months in, there is still no congressional authorization, and the White House's argument that the War Powers Resolution's 60-day clock stopped at the April ceasefire is doing a lot of work. Schiff, Kaine and Schumer are pressing another War Powers vote. Just Security frames the tanker exchanges as evidence the “hostilities ended” theory has collapsed. The broader critique: a war of attrition with no defined end state, escalating by reflex.

Right view

Notably, the sharpest skepticism is coming from the right, not just the left. National Review has run pieces arguing the Iran war is “eating Trump's presidency” and that his adversaries have concluded he is bluffing — questioning whether he has the patience for the economic-pressure campaign he announced. Washington Examiner coverage ties voter fatigue to the midterms. Fox News and administration allies counter that proportional retaliation is the only language Tehran responds to, and that backing off now would invite more attacks on US ships. Al Jazeera's opinion page has carried the case that the strategy is starting to pay off.

Watch for

Analysts at Sparta and the Stimson Center warn that a Hormuz disruption sustained through Q3 puts roughly 12 million bpd of export supply at risk and could drive a shallow global recession in the second half of 2026. Near-term markers: whether Iran strikes a US-flagged vessel (a likely escalation trigger), whether Gulf states permit further use of their airspace, and whether the next War Powers vote draws Republican defectors. Freight and war-risk premiums on Gulf routes are the cleanest real-time gauge of how the market reads the risk.

Sources: Al Jazeera Axios NPR CNN National Review Just Security Stimson

Brent touches $100 and gas sets a September record — and the Fed is now expected to hike

Facts

  • Brent crude rose about 2.3% early Wednesday to briefly trade at $100 a barrel, its first time there since July, per CNN Business. WTI was up about 1.3% near $94.
  • Brent and WTI are each up more than 60% year to date.
  • AAA puts the national average for regular at roughly $4.13–$4.15 a gallon — the highest ever recorded for September. Diesel hit a record $5.90 on Tuesday.
  • J.P. Morgan Wealth Management now expects a 25-basis-point hike at the September FOMC meeting, a reversal from its prior call of no changes in 2026. Futures markets put the odds near 57%.
  • July CPI ran at 3.4%, up from 2.7% a year earlier. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks were read as hawkish.

Left view

MSNBC and Democratic messaging tie the pump price directly to the decision to go to war with Iran — a cost imposed by choice, not by circumstance. The Christian Science Monitor's reporting notes voters are feeling the squeeze eight weeks from an election. The framing: an administration that campaigned on lowering prices has delivered a war that raises them, and is now forcing the Fed into hikes that will slow hiring on top of it.

Right view

Fox News opinion argues voters judge the economy by their “personal economy” — groceries, gas, mortgage rates — and concedes those numbers are bad for the GOP right now. The Washington Times went further, calling the economy a warning bell for Trump and Republicans in the midterms. The defensive case from administration allies: the supply shock is Tehran's doing, domestic production is being expanded, and the Fed's credibility problem predates the war. Reason and other libertarian outlets fold tariffs into the price story as a self-inflicted addition.

Watch for

Chase and J.P. Morgan strategists flag $120 Brent as the level where the shock stops being manageable and starts threatening growth. Watch the September FOMC decision, the next CPI print, and whether SPR releases or an OPEC+ response materialize. Historically, the president's party has lost an average of 32 House seats in midterms held when gas is expensive — a statistic both parties are now quoting.

Sources: CNN Business AAA J.P. Morgan / Chase CNBC Fox News CS Monitor

Canada's counter-tariffs take effect on roughly $20B of American goods

Facts

  • Canada's retaliatory tariffs took effect just after midnight ET Tuesday, covering hundreds of product categories. Ottawa's own accounting puts the figure at $27.6 billion CAD; US reporting generally cites roughly $20 billion.
  • Rates run from 15% to 50%. At 50%: American milk, perfume, video game consoles, golf clubs, fishing rods, steel, aluminum, jackets and T-shirts. At 25%: cheese, carpets, stoves and air conditioners. At 15%: forklifts and industrial molds.
  • The measures answer the Trump administration's 50% duties on about $20 billion of Canadian goods, imposed after trade talks broke down in August.
  • Canada also announced a $7.5 billion support package for affected businesses and workers.
  • Context: the Supreme Court's 6–3 ruling in Learning Resources v. Trump (February) held that IEEPA does not authorize presidential tariffs, invalidating that category. Section 232 tariffs — the authority behind the steel and aluminum duties — survived and are what's in play here.

Left view

The Guardian and Vox treat this as the predictable end of a trade strategy built on leverage the courts partly took away: after IEEPA was struck down, the administration narrowed to Section 232, allies retaliated, and American consumers pay twice. The Tax Policy Center's analysis is cited to argue the relief from the Supreme Court ruling is smaller than advertised because the remaining tariffs still bite.

Right view

Reason ran the story straight and critically — libertarian outlets have been the most consistent conservative opponents of the tariffs throughout. The Tax Foundation, which leans free-market, welcomed the IEEPA ruling as a rebuke of executive overreach and estimates the invalidated tariffs would have shrunk long-run GDP by 0.3%. Trade-hawk voices at the Washington Examiner and OANN frame Canadian retaliation as proof Ottawa was never bargaining in good faith and argue holding firm is the only way to reset terms.

Watch for

PwC and Norton Rose Fulbright estimate up to $175 billion in potential IEEPA refunds working through the system — a real fiscal item. Watch whether the administration reaches for other trade authorities to rebuild what the Court took down, whether Canadian retaliation broadens to energy or procurement, and how the 50% duties land on Midwest agriculture and appliance manufacturing heading into November.

Sources: CNBC Dept. of Finance Canada Reason Tax Foundation PwC

Twelve countries move to ban Israeli settlement goods; Israel closes the UK consulate in East Jerusalem

Facts

  • The UK, France and Canada announced Tuesday they will ban imports of goods produced in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and Jewish neighborhoods of East Jerusalem. Goods from Israel proper are not affected.
  • Nine more countries — Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden — said they will introduce national restrictions, back EU-level measures, or actively consider them. Three of the twelve are G7 members.
  • The joint foreign ministers' statement cited unprecedented settler violence and continued settlement expansion as undermining a two-state solution.
  • Israel condemned the move and announced retaliation, including closing the British consulate in East Jerusalem. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced the countermeasures; President Isaac Herzog also objected, as did US Ambassador Mike Huckabee.
  • France is separately pushing for an EU-wide ban.

Left view

NPR led with the UK's language accusing Israeli settlers of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. The Guardian and Chatham House frame the bans as long overdue — the point being that decades of statements condemning settlements as illegal under international law finally carry an economic cost. Supporters emphasize the narrow scope: this targets settlements, not Israel.

Right view

The Free Press, National Review and the NY Post treat the distinction between “settlements” and “Israel” as thinner than advertised, and read the timing — with Israel's principal ally at war with Iran — as European governments responding to domestic political pressure rather than events on the ground. Israeli right-wing politicians and Huckabee argue the bans reward intransigence and remove any incentive for Palestinian negotiation. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency's coverage documents the reaction across the Israeli political spectrum, where opposition was broad.

Watch for

Whether the EU adopts a bloc-wide measure, which would change the scale materially — settlement exports to the UK alone are small, in the low tens of millions annually, so the near-term economic bite is symbolic. Watch for further Israeli countermeasures beyond the consulate closure, whether Washington pressures allies to reverse, and whether more countries join the twelve.

Sources: NPR TIME JTA ABC (Australia) Chatham House Euronews

Midterm season opens with control of Congress genuinely in play

Facts

  • Labor Day marked the unofficial start of the general election season. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are up on November 3.
  • Democrats need to flip three seats to take the House. Republicans are defending a 53-seat Senate majority.
  • Trump's approval sits near 38%, with Democrats holding roughly a 6-point lead on the generic congressional ballot, per NPR's summary of the polling averages.
  • Decision Desk HQ has moved its Senate forecast to an even 50–50, with movement toward Democrats in Alaska, Maine, Ohio and Texas. Prediction markets put a Democratic sweep near 50%.
  • Congress passed a stopgap on Sept. 2 funding agencies through Dec. 11, avoiding a shutdown; the House vote was 370–48.

Left view

NPR and MSNBC read the environment as a classic midterm backlash amplified by two unpopular decisions — the war and the tariffs — that both show up in prices. The Christian Science Monitor's reporting on the gas-price effect is the mechanism Democrats are leaning on. A data point Democrats highlight: voters say they trust their party more than Republicans on the economy for the first time since 2010.

Right view

Fox News' Power Rankings put the economy, health care and inflation as the top three issues and treat the map as difficult but not lost, noting the Senate's favorable geography for the GOP. The Washington Times is more direct that the economy is a warning bell. The Dispatch and National Review have argued Trump has forfeited his strongest issue — economic stewardship — by pursuing tariffs and the war simultaneously. Conservative counter-argument: Democratic economic messaging still polls poorly, and a 6-point generic lead in September has evaporated before.

Watch for

Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin and 270toWin both have the House leaning Democratic and the Senate as a coin flip. Structurally, the House is the likelier flip because the threshold is three seats; the Senate depends on whether the Alaska, Maine, Ohio and Texas races hold their current trajectory. Watch the December 11 funding deadline — it lands after the election and before the new Congress, which is where a shutdown fight would have maximum leverage and minimum accountability.

Sources: NPR Silver Bulletin Fox News Washington Times 270toWin

NTSB interviews crew of Amazon cargo jet that overran a Miami runway, killing five

Facts

  • Prime Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 from San Juan, overran the runway at Miami International around 2 p.m. Sunday, tore through a perimeter fence and struck vehicles on NW 67th Avenue. Five people died, five were injured.
  • All the victims were in vehicles on the road, not aboard the aircraft, the NTSB said.
  • The aircraft came to rest roughly 1,300 feet past the paved runway. Video appears to show it remaining airborne well down the runway before touchdown.
  • Investigators are examining touchdown point, speed, braking, weather and wind, and the aircraft's mechanical condition. Crew interviews began this week, along with interviews of controllers and dispatchers.
  • Miami International does not have engineered materials arrestor beds — crushable pads designed to stop overrunning aircraft.

Left view

NPR and coverage in left-leaning outlets center the arrestor-bed gap and the broader question of aviation infrastructure funding, alongside scrutiny of contracted air-cargo operations and crew scheduling pressure at Amazon's air network. The framing: a known, engineerable risk that money would have mitigated.

Right view

Right-leaning coverage at the NY Post and Fox has stayed largely on the reporting rather than the policy, with commentary cautioning against drawing regulatory conclusions before the NTSB establishes cause — noting that early video suggesting a long landing points to flight-crew factors rather than infrastructure. Some conservative aviation commentators fold this into ongoing criticism of FAA staffing and air-traffic modernization delays.

Watch for

The NTSB preliminary report, typically within 30 days, which should establish touchdown point and whether the aircraft was configured and braking normally. If a long landing is confirmed, expect renewed pressure on the FAA over runway safety areas at airports where geography makes standard overrun zones impossible — Miami among them. Amazon Air's operational model and its contract carriers are likely to draw congressional attention regardless of cause.

Sources: NPR CNBC CBS Miami ABC News

Markets & Economy

  • S&P 500: closed Tuesday at 7,673.52, down 0.58%; up about 0.1% early Wednesday. Dow: 52,786.07, down 628.18 points or 1.18% Tuesday. Nasdaq: 26,421.41, down 0.32%.
  • Oil: Brent briefly $100/bbl Wednesday, first time since July; WTI near $94. Both up more than 60% year to date.
  • Gas: AAA national average about $4.13–$4.15 for regular — a record for September. Diesel set an all-time high of $5.90 on Tuesday.
  • Rates: Markets price roughly 57% odds of a 25bp hike at the September FOMC; J.P. Morgan Wealth Management has flipped its base case to a hike. July CPI 3.4%.
  • Other: Fox News parted ways with anchor Maria Bartiromo after more than 12 years, effective immediately; her attorney disputes reports she was fired. Shipping war-risk premiums on Gulf routes remain the market's live gauge of Hormuz risk.

Sports Watercooler

  • Golf: Scottie Scheffler took his second FedExCup title — his 22nd PGA Tour win and third of the season. Attention shifts to the Presidents Cup at Medinah outside Chicago, Brandt Snedeker vs. Geoff Ogilvy. The FedExCup Fall opens with two new stops: the Biltmore Championship in Asheville and the Good Good Championship in Austin.
  • Tennis: An American man will play in the US Open final for the first time since 2006 — Ben Shelton beat Carlos Alcaraz in five (7-6 in the fifth) and Frances Tiafoe came back from two sets down against Alex Michelsen. They meet in the semifinal. On the women's side, Aryna Sabalenka survived Linda Nosková and faces Jessica Pegula, who beat Emma Navarro 3-6, 6-4, 6-3. Muchová and Menšík already have the mixed doubles title.
  • Squash: Paul Coll won the London Squash Classic over Joel Makin 13-11, 11-7, 11-8. Tour events run this week in Hong Kong and Maspeth, NY, with the season's first Platinum event — the QTerminals Qatar Classic in Doha — starting September 12.
  • WWE: CM Punk retained the Undisputed WWE Title against Johnny Gargano on Friday's SmackDown despite Sami Zayn's interference, then challenged Zayn to a title match in Mexico City. WWE announced eight new Raw and SmackDown dates; presale opens Thursday, general sale Friday.
  • Hockey: Rookie camps are open, with the prospect showcases running September 11-15 and veteran camps opening the 16th and 17th. Preseason games start September 19; the regular season opens September 29 — the first year of the 84-game schedule under the new CBA. Toronto has No. 1 pick Gavin McKenna and newly signed Sergei Bobrovsky. Dylan Larkin and Connor Hellebuyck remain the names in trade speculation.
  • Soccer: The Champions League league phase begins this week. In the Premier League, Arsenal opened their title defense against promoted Coventry City back on August 21. World Cup qualifying is done — the 48-team field for the North American tournament is set.
  • Football: College football's first full Saturday delivered LSU routing Clemson, Colorado edging Georgia Tech 14-13, Houston over Oregon State 33-20, and West Virginia past Coastal Carolina 31-24. Notre Dame played Wisconsin at Lambeau, and Ole Miss met Louisville in a Top 25 game Sunday. NFL Week 1 is underway.

item.title: Tue Sep 8, 2026 — Two Saudi supertankers hit near Hormuz as the US–Iran shipping war widens
item.description: Two Saudi supertankers hit near Hormuz as the US–Iran shipping war widens · Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect today · Gas at $4.15 pushes inflation to a three-year high, and the Fed meets next week · New Hampshire votes today in the first big primary of the fall
item.content:encoded:
The Big Stories Today

Two Saudi supertankers hit near Hormuz as the US–Iran shipping war widens

Facts

  • Two supertankers carrying Saudi crude were struck by projectiles within minutes of each other late Monday while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz, and a Saudi Aramco facility was reportedly hit in a separate attack. No party had claimed responsibility as of this morning.
  • Brent crude climbed roughly 1.5% to about $97.73 a barrel, a six-week high.
  • The strikes follow CENTCOM's disabling of three Iranian crude carriers — near Kharg Island, off Jask, and in the Gulf of Oman — on Sept. 5, which the command said was retaliation for IRGC ballistic missiles fired at two US Navy warships. CENTCOM described the tankers as part of a shadow fleet funding the IRGC and its proxies.
  • The US naval blockade of Iranian ports remains in force and Hormuz transits remain severely constrained. Trump has said repeatedly since August that a deal to reopen the strait "could be soon."

Left view

NPR and The Guardian frame this as an open-ended war that Congress has never authorized, now spilling into commercial shipping lanes with no stated endpoint. The Kaine–Paul war powers resolution failed 47–53 in the Senate in March, and left-leaning outlets argue that vote effectively handed the administration a blank check — one now being spent on strikes against civilian-flagged vessels.

Right view

Fox News coverage centers on Vice President Vance's argument that US military pressure has prevented an energy crisis rather than caused one, and that hitting the IRGC's tanker revenue is the cheapest available way to degrade Iran without ground troops. National Review-style hawks add that Tehran's willingness to strike Saudi cargo shows the blockade is working. A libertarian minority (Reason, Rand Paul) still objects that this is a war Congress never declared.

Watch for

The EIA's August outlook pencils Brent at roughly $85 for Q3 and $87 for full-year 2026 — today's spot price is well above both, so either the forecast rises again or traders expect de-escalation. Analysts broadly expect prices to stay elevated until Gulf flows normalize and inventories rebuild, with most regional production seen returning near pre-conflict levels in early 2027. Near term: whether Saudi Arabia reroutes cargo through the East–West pipeline, whether insurers pull war-risk cover for Hormuz transits, and whether Friday's CPI print forces the Fed's hand.

Sources: CNN NPR CNBC Fox News Military Times EIA

Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect today

Facts

  • Canadian counter-tariffs on roughly C$27.6 billion (about US$20 billion) of American goods take effect today, applying duties of 15%, 25% and 50% across roughly 700 product lines.
  • Targets include US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics — a list built to match Washington dollar-for-dollar.
  • The measures answer a 50% US levy on $20 billion of Canadian goods imposed last month after negotiations collapsed. Ottawa said the final US terms undercut the net benefit to Canada and called into question whether any deal would hold.
  • Trump has threatened further escalation: barring sales of Bombardier aircraft, and raising tariffs on Canada-built cars and auto parts from 25% to 50% starting in January.

Left view

The Washington Post and The Guardian emphasize that talks broke down because US conditions kept moving, not because Canada walked. Their framing is that tariffs are a consumption tax landing on American buyers of Canadian steel and aluminum, and that a durable trading relationship is being spent for leverage that has not produced a deal in eight months.

Right view

The right is genuinely split here. Fox Business and administration allies argue Canada blinks eventually and that January's auto escalation is the pressure point. But the free-trade right — the WSJ editorial board, National Review, Reason — has been among the sharpest critics, calling tariffs a self-inflicted tax on US manufacturers and warning that the auto supply chain crossing the border multiple times makes a 50% duty a tax on American assembly plants.

Watch for

Auto and steel equities today; Canadian dollar; whether provinces add non-tariff measures such as procurement bans or liquor delistings, which they used in 2025. The January auto escalation is the real cliff — economists on both sides expect the bulk of the GDP hit to land in Q1 2027, not now. Also watch the USMCA review calendar and any signal that Ottawa seeks WTO or Chapter 31 arbitration.

Sources: Washington Post Bloomberg The Hill ABC News TIME

Gas at $4.15 pushes inflation to a three-year high, and the Fed meets next week

Facts

  • AAA's national average for regular sits at about $4.15 a gallon, roughly a dollar higher than a month ago. California is highest at about $5.81; Indiana lowest at about $3.45.
  • PBS NewsHour reported that spiking gasoline prices pushed headline inflation to its highest level in three years last month.
  • The Fed held the funds rate at 3.50%–3.75% in July for a fifth straight meeting, but three FOMC members dissented in favor of a 25bp hike. Markets have moved from pricing 2026 cuts to pricing a hike.
  • August's jobs report came in strong, removing one argument against tightening. A fresh CPI reading lands Friday.

Left view

NPR and Vox frame the pump price as the domestic bill for the Gulf campaign: an energy shock that is regressive by construction, hitting rural and exurban drivers with long commutes hardest, and one that monetary policy cannot fix because the Fed cannot manufacture crude. The Atlantic's version of the argument is that an administration running on affordability is now the proximate cause of the affordability problem.

Right view

Fox News and the Washington Examiner put the causation on Tehran, not Washington — Iran is choking a waterway, and the fix is supply: faster permitting, more domestic drilling, LNG approvals, and refinery capacity. The Wall Street Journal editorial board has made a narrower point, that a supply shock is exactly the kind of inflation the Fed should look through rather than hike into.

Watch for

Friday's CPI is the pivot. CNBC's reporting earlier this year argued $4 gas would not by itself trigger hikes because energy shocks are demand-destructive, but the July dissents and a hot jobs print have shifted that calculus. A hike into an energy shock eight weeks before the midterms would be extraordinary; holding while headline inflation runs at a three-year high invites the opposite criticism. Watch the 2-year yield and Fed funds futures for the market's read.

Sources: AAA PBS NewsHour Federal Reserve CNBC Choose Energy

New Hampshire votes today in the first big primary of the fall

Facts

  • New Hampshire holds its state primary today, September 8. Delaware follows on September 15; the general election is November 3.
  • The Senate seat is open — Jeanne Shaheen announced in early 2025 that she would not seek re-election.
  • Democratic primary: Rep. Chris Pappas and Karishma Manzur. Republican primary: former Sen. Scott Brown, former Sen. John Sununu, Charlie Hough and Tejasinha Sivalingam.
  • Separately, the administration is compiling state-by-state lists of citizens eligible to vote but will not meet its own 60-days-before-Election-Day deadline.

Left view

NPR's election coverage treats New Hampshire as a must-hold in a cycle where Democrats have almost no margin, and points to Michigan — where a bruising primary left the party trying to reunify — as the cautionary case. On the voter-list project, left-leaning outlets frame a federal registry of eligible voters as a durable infrastructure risk regardless of who runs it.

Right view

Fox News and the Washington Examiner see an open seat in a state Republicans have won statewide before, with two former senators competing on name recognition, and argue affordability and gas prices give the GOP a lane even in a blue-trending state. On the voter lists, right-leaning outlets frame it as routine list maintenance and note the missed deadline undercuts claims of an imminent power grab.

Watch for

Turnout in Hillsborough and Rockingham counties as a read on GOP enthusiasm; the Brown–Sununu margin, since a bloodied winner starts the general at a cash disadvantage. Forecasters have treated New Hampshire as lean-Democratic; a close primary and a gas-price-driven affordability message are the two things that would move it. Data centers (below) are already showing up in New England ad buys.

Sources: Ballotpedia NPR NH Bulletin CNN Citizens Count

Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon test a ceasefire that never fully held

Facts

  • At least 27 people have been killed in Israeli strikes across southern Lebanon over three days, according to Lebanese authorities.
  • Monday's strikes in Kfar Rumman killed 12, including a paramedic and, per Lebanon's Ministry of Public Health, at least four women and two children in a targeted residential building.
  • CNBC reported Israel–Hezbollah clashes killing 11 as regional escalation accelerated following the US–Iran exchanges.
  • President Joseph Aoun holds Israel responsible, calls the Nabatieh assault a dangerous escalation, and has asked Washington and the international community to intervene. The US-brokered conditional ceasefire took effect in late June and has never produced a full halt.

Left view

The Guardian, Al Jazeera and Common Dreams argue the word "ceasefire" no longer describes the situation — strikes on residential buildings, paramedics and health facilities are the pattern, not the exception, and Washington's leverage as guarantor is going unused. Note that mainstream US coverage of the Lebanon front has been thin this week relative to the Iran story.

Right view

Fox News and the New York Post frame the strikes as enforcement rather than escalation: Hezbollah has used the ceasefire to rearm through Syrian and Iranian supply lines, the Lebanese Armed Forces have not disarmed the south as the agreement required, and Israel is acting where the guarantor mechanism failed. The Free Press adds that the Lebanon front cannot be separated from the Iran campaign — the same command structure runs both.

Watch for

Whether Washington sends an envoy to Beirut, which has been the pattern before each previous de-escalation. Also: UNIFIL's posture, whether Hezbollah responds with rocket fire into northern Israel (which would end the ceasefire outright), and whether Lebanon's fragile currency and banking recovery takes another hit. Analysts widely expect Lebanon to remain the secondary front for as long as the Gulf campaign continues.

Sources: CNBC Al Jazeera Common Dreams Reuters via Yahoo

Data centers become the rare issue both parties are running against

Facts

  • Campaigns and outside groups have spent more than $45 million since January on ads mentioning data centers, across gubernatorial, House and Senate races.
  • Both parties are making substantially the same argument: the facilities take too many tax breaks, raise electricity bills, and need reining in.
  • Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong and Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy have both called for moratoriums.
  • Public opinion has swung from cautiously optimistic to largely negative, with concerns about electricity rates, water use and overstated job numbers cutting across party lines.

Left view

NPR and Mother Jones frame it as a straightforward corporate-subsidy story: ratepayers absorb grid upgrades and higher bills so that a handful of trillion-dollar companies can build, while the promised permanent jobs number in the dozens. Vox adds the water angle in drought-exposed counties.

Right view

The populist right — and Ramaswamy is the clearest example — runs on local control, land use and the unfairness of targeted tax abatements. But the pro-growth right splits sharply: The Dispatch and the WSJ editorial page warn that a wave of local moratoriums would hand the AI buildout to jurisdictions with looser rules, and that the electricity problem is a supply failure caused by a decade of blocked generation, not by the customers.

Watch for

State public utility commission rate cases are where this actually gets decided, not campaign ads. CNBC has noted the market risk directly: losses for pro-data-center candidates would fuel more moratoriums, which threaten the AI capex cycle that a large share of 2026 index gains rest on. Watch Virginia, Ohio, Georgia and Wisconsin, and watch whether hyperscalers start pre-announcing ratepayer-protection deals to defuse the issue before November.

Sources: NPR CNN CNBC Brookings NBC News

Nepal–Tibet flood toll passes 1,380 with about 5,500 still missing

Facts

  • At least 1,384 people have been confirmed killed across Nepal and China — 1,341 bodies recovered in Nepal, 43 deaths in Tibet.
  • More than 5,500 people remain missing, including roughly 800 foreign nationals: about 4,996 in Nepal and 519 in Tibet.
  • Authorities believe a glacial collapse triggered the flooding. Two survivors were pulled from debris in separate operations ten days in, well past the usual survival window.
  • CNN reported that warning signs were visible before the disaster, citing an assessment of the glacial lake and monitoring gaps.

Left view

The Guardian and NPR connect the glacial collapse to accelerating high-altitude warming and argue the story is a preview: the Himalayan glacial-lake outburst risk is known, mapped, and largely unfunded. UN agencies have used the toll to press wealthy states on adaptation and loss-and-damage financing.

Right view

Right-leaning outlets have given this comparatively little coverage; where they have engaged, the framing is that attributing a single glacial collapse to climate policy failure outruns the evidence, and that the operative failure was local — monitoring, early warning and building in floodplains — not a global emissions ledger. Reason's version: adaptation spending beats treaty commitments.

Watch for

The transition from rescue to recovery, which usually collapses the "missing" number sharply and raises the confirmed toll. Watch the UN flash appeal funding level, whether China permits broader access to the Tibetan side, and the monsoon-season assessment of remaining unstable glacial lakes upstream. Nepal's tourism season, a meaningful share of GDP, is the second-order economic story.

Sources: Al Jazeera ABC News UN News CNN

Markets & Economy

  • S&P 500: futures off about 0.2% pre-open. Dow: futures down about 0.7%. Nasdaq: Nasdaq-100 futures just below flat. US markets were closed Monday for Labor Day; in Friday's session the Dow fell 0.51%, the S&P 500 0.38% and the Nasdaq Composite 0.29%.
  • Oil: Brent up about 1.5% to roughly $97.73, a six-week high, on the Hormuz tanker strikes and the reported Aramco hit. EIA's August outlook had Brent averaging about $85 in Q3 and $87 for 2026 — spot is running well ahead of both.
  • Gas: AAA national average about $4.15/gal, up roughly $1 in a month. California $5.81, Indiana $3.45.
  • Other: Friday's CPI is the week's main event, with markets pricing a live September Fed meeting after three July dissents favored a hike. Oracle earnings land later this week as the AI-capex bellwether. Canada's counter-tariffs bite steel, autos and appliances from today. And the Seattle Times and Newsday sued OpenAI and Microsoft on Friday in the Southern District of New York, alleging their journalism — including paywalled articles — was scraped for training data; they are seeking destruction of the datasets and models involved. OpenAI cites fair use; Microsoft said it was surprised and open to talks.

Sports Watercooler

  • Golf: Scottie Scheffler closed out the Tour Championship at −16, three clear of Viktor Hovland. FedExCup Fall opens next week with the new Biltmore Championship in Asheville (Sept. 14–20), then the Presidents Cup at Medinah, Sept. 21–27 — Brandt Snedeker captaining the US against Geoff Ogilvy's Internationals.
  • Tennis: US Open week two. Carlos Alcaraz (defending) reached the men's quarters alongside Ben Shelton, Frances Tiafoe and Alex Michelsen — three Americans in the last eight. Coco Gauff is back in the women's quarters; Naomi Osaka is out. Karolína Muchová and Jakub Menšík took the mixed doubles title over Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli.
  • Squash: The London Squash Classic at Alexandra Palace wrapped Sept. 6 as the season's first televised event. Next up is the season's first Platinum, the QTerminals Qatar Classic in Doha, Sept. 12–18. The Swedish Open returns to the tour Sept. 30–Oct. 4 for the first time since 2018; PSA has 24 events across 14 countries booked through December.
  • WWE: Raw came from Birmingham on Labor Day with Money in the Bank qualifiers and Liv Morgan vs. Stephanie Vaquer, plus fallout from Sunday's Main Event. Both brands head to Mexico City this month — SmackDown on the 11th, Raw on the 14th.
  • Hockey: Rookie and prospect camps open this week, feeding into the rookie showcases Sept. 11–15; veteran camps open roughly Sept. 10–13. Opening night is Sept. 29, with Carolina hosting Florida, Montreal at Toronto and the Rangers at Boston — the first 84-game regular season. Storylines: the defending-champion Hurricanes managing a title hangover, Toronto pairing No. 1 pick Gavin McKenna with new signing Sergei Bobrovsky, and Patrick Kane back in Chicago on a two-year deal.
  • Soccer: A full slate of UEFA World Cup qualifiers today at 2:45 p.m. ET — Israel vs. Italy is the headline, with Croatia–Montenegro, Greece–Denmark, Switzerland–Slovenia, Belarus–Scotland, Kosovo–Sweden and Gibraltar–Faroe Islands alongside. Europe has 16 places; 12 group winners go direct and the rest fight through playoffs.
  • Football: The NFL season kicks off tomorrow night, Patriots at Seahawks, 8:20 p.m. ET on NBC. The 49ers visit the Rams Thursday on Netflix, and the main Week 1 Sunday slate follows on the 13th.

item.title: Mon Sep 7, 2026 — Witkoff and Kushner carry a peace framework from Moscow to Kyiv
item.description: Witkoff and Kushner carry a peace framework from Moscow to Kyiv · Armed man lunges at Ohio Democratic nominee Amy Acton at the Canfield Fair · AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt outright but falls short of a governing majority · The Fed edges toward a rate hike as the White House mounts a public pressure campaign
item.content:encoded:
The Big Stories Today

Witkoff and Kushner carry a peace framework from Moscow to Kyiv

Facts

  • Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Friday, then traveled overland from Rzeszow, Poland to Kyiv, arriving Sunday.
  • They met twice with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his senior advisers; national security advisers from the UK, France and Germany joined a third session.
  • The envoys said afterward they were encouraged by the discussion and expected further progress. No terms have been published.
  • Russia and Ukraine agreed to pause aerial attacks on each other's capitals for the duration of the visits. There is no broader ceasefire.
  • The war is in its fifth year. Momentum on talks had stalled for months while Washington was consumed by the Iran conflict.

Left view

NPR and The Washington Post frame the trip as a genuine but fragile opening, and stress that the pause in capital strikes is a diplomatic courtesy rather than a ceasefire. Al Jazeera and center-left analysts note the visit followed Putin's own public claim that a deal is possible, and read that as a familiar pattern — Moscow signaling flexibility to keep talks alive without conceding anything concrete. PBS NewsHour has reported Ukrainian and European leaders accusing Putin of stalling and rejecting land-for-peace terms outright.

Right view

Coverage on the right is split rather than unified. The Washington Times treats the Kyiv stop as evidence the administration is the only party actually moving the war toward an end. But Republican unease is on the record: Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) has called the territorial elements of the US framework appeasement, and polling from the right-leaning Vandenberg Coalition found only about 16% of Trump voters back Ukraine ceding territory while roughly 76% favor sanctioning Russia. The Atlantic Council's UkraineAlert argues Putin cannot accept any settlement that preserves real Ukrainian statehood, and that pressure works better than offers.

Watch for

Whether the aerial pause over Kyiv and Moscow holds past the envoys' departure is the near-term tell — analysts expect a resumption within days if no framework is agreed. Watch for a published term sheet, and specifically for language on NATO membership, force caps and de facto recognition of occupied territory, each of which European capitals have signaled they will not endorse. Energy desks see limited crude reaction from Ukraine headlines right now; the Middle East is the dominant risk premium. A visible breakdown would likely revive the sanctions track instead, which is where congressional Republicans have said they prefer to be.

Sources: Washington Post NPR Axios Al Jazeera Washington Times Atlantic Council

Armed man lunges at Ohio Democratic nominee Amy Acton at the Canfield Fair

Facts

  • The incident happened around 2:30 p.m. Sunday at the Canfield Fair in Canfield, Ohio, outside Youngstown, while Acton was campaigning.
  • Patrick Havas, 38, was arrested by the Mahoning County Sheriff's Office and is expected to face two assault charges and one count of disorderly conduct.
  • Deputies recovered two firearms and brass knuckles on Havas. Law enforcement says neither firearm was brandished during the incident.
  • Acton, a physician and former state health director, was not hurt. Two older adults were knocked down; Acton stayed on site and attended to one of the injured.
